blocks.body:
The Riemann zeta function packages the primes of $\mathbb Z$: $\zeta(s) = \sum_n n^{-s} = \prod_p(1 - p^{-s})^{-1}$, and the Euler product is just unique factorization written analytically (see [[zeta]]). A number field $K$ has its own "integers" $\mathcal O_K$ and its own primes, the prime ideals, and unique factorization of ideals (see [[ideals]]) gives an Euler product in exactly the same way. The result is the Dedekind zeta function $\zeta_K(s)$.

Its value lies in two facts. First, for quadratic fields (and more generally abelian fields) it factors into $\zeta(s)$ times Dirichlet $L$-functions, so questions about primes and ideals in $K$ become questions about characters on $\mathbb Z$. Second, its residue at $s = 1$ contains the class number, the regulator and the discriminant of $K$, which is how class numbers are computed and estimated.

blocks.title: Dedekind zeta function
blocks.body:
For a number field $K$ of degree $n$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,s > 1$,
$$\zeta_K(s) = \sum_{\mathfrak a \ne 0} N\mathfrak a^{-s} = \sum_{m=1}^\infty \frac{a_K(m)}{m^s}, \qquad a_K(m) = \#\{\mathfrak a \subseteq \mathcal O_K : N\mathfrak a = m\},$$
the sum running over nonzero ideals of $\mathcal O_K$, where $N\mathfrak a = |\mathcal O_K/\mathfrak a|$.

For $K = \mathbb Q$ the ideals are $(m)$, $m \ge 1$, and $\zeta_{\mathbb Q} = \zeta$. The coefficients count ideals, not elements.

blocks.title: Euler product
blocks.body:
For real $\sigma > 1$ the series converges, with $\zeta_K(\sigma) \le \zeta(\sigma)^n$, and for $\mathrm{Re}\,s > 1$ it converges absolutely and
$$\zeta_K(s) = \prod_{\mathfrak p}\bigl(1 - N\mathfrak p^{-s}\bigr)^{-1},$$
the product running over nonzero prime ideals. In particular $\zeta_K(s) \ne 0$ for $\mathrm{Re}\,s > 1$.

Each nonzero prime ideal $\mathfrak p$ contains exactly one rational prime $p$ (namely $\mathfrak p \cap \mathbb Z = p\mathbb Z$), so $\mathfrak p$ divides $p\mathcal O_K$ and $N\mathfrak p = p^f$ with $f \ge 1$. Writing $p\mathcal O_K = \prod\mathfrak p_i^{e_i}$ and taking norms, $\sum e_if_i = n$ because $N(p\mathcal O_K) = p^n$. So at most $n$ prime ideals lie above $p$, and for real $\sigma > 1$
$$\prod_{\mathfrak p \mid p}\bigl(1 - N\mathfrak p^{-\sigma}\bigr)^{-1} \le \bigl(1 - p^{-\sigma}\bigr)^{-n}.$$

Fix $x$ and expand the finite product over the prime ideals of norm at most $x$ into geometric series. By unique factorization of ideals and multiplicativity of the norm, every ideal $\mathfrak a$ built from these primes appears exactly once, contributing $N\mathfrak a^{-\sigma}$; in particular every ideal of norm at most $x$ appears. Hence
$$\sum_{N\mathfrak a \le x} N\mathfrak a^{-\sigma} \le \prod_{N\mathfrak p \le x}\bigl(1 - N\mathfrak p^{-\sigma}\bigr)^{-1} \le \prod_{p \le x}\bigl(1 - p^{-\sigma}\bigr)^{-n} \le \zeta(\sigma)^n.$$
So the series converges absolutely for $\mathrm{Re}\,s > 1$, and the difference between the partial product and the full series is bounded by the tail $\sum_{N\mathfrak a > x}N\mathfrak a^{-\sigma}$, which tends to $0$. A convergent product of nonzero factors with $\sum |N\mathfrak p^{-s}| < \infty$ is nonzero.

blocks.title: The Gaussian example
blocks.body:
Take $K = \mathbb Q(i)$, $\mathcal O_K = \mathbb Z[i]$. From the factorization of primes in the [[gaussian-integers]], the Euler factors at a rational prime $p$ are:

- $p = 2 = -i(1+i)^2$: one prime of norm $2$, factor $(1 - 2^{-s})^{-1}$;
- $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $p = \pi\bar\pi$: two primes of norm $p$, factor $(1 - p^{-s})^{-2}$;
- $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, inert: one prime of norm $p^2$, factor $(1 - p^{-2s})^{-1} = (1 - p^{-s})^{-1}(1 + p^{-s})^{-1}$.

Let $\chi_{-4}$ be the character modulo $4$ with $\chi_{-4}(n) = 1, 0, -1, 0$ for $n \equiv 1, 2, 3, 0$. In every case the Euler factor equals $(1 - p^{-s})^{-1}(1 - \chi_{-4}(p)p^{-s})^{-1}$, so
$$\zeta_{\mathbb Q(i)}(s) = \zeta(s)\,L(s, \chi_{-4}).$$
Comparing Dirichlet coefficients, $a_K(m) = \sum_{d \mid m}\chi_{-4}(d)$. Since every ideal of $\mathbb Z[i]$ is principal with four generators, this says $r_2(m) = 4\sum_{d \mid m}\chi_{-4}(d)$, the classical formula for the number of ways to write $m$ as a sum of two squares.

blocks.title: Factorization for quadratic fields
blocks.body:
Let $K$ be a quadratic field of discriminant $D$ (so $K = \mathbb Q(\sqrt D)$, with $D = d$ if $d \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $D = 4d$ otherwise, $d$ squarefree), and let $\chi_D(m) = \left(\frac Dm\right)$ be the Kronecker symbol, a primitive real character modulo $|D|$. Then
$$\zeta_{\mathbb Q(\sqrt D)}(s) = \zeta(s)\, L(s, \chi_D), \qquad a_K(m) = \sum_{d \mid m}\chi_D(d).$$

The splitting law for quadratic fields says that a rational prime $p$ splits into two distinct primes of norm $p$ when $\chi_D(p) = 1$, stays prime (norm $p^2$) when $\chi_D(p) = -1$, and ramifies ($p\mathcal O_K = \mathfrak p^2$, $N\mathfrak p = p$) when $\chi_D(p) = 0$, i.e. $p \mid D$. For odd $p$ this is the Dedekind–Kummer theorem applied to $x^2 - d$, since $\chi_D(p) = \left(\frac dp\right)$ (when $d \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, $\mathbb Z[\sqrt d]$ has index $2$ in $\mathcal O_K$, which does not matter for odd $p$). For $p = 2$ and $D = 4d$, $x^2 - d$ is $x^2$ or $(x+1)^2$ modulo $2$, so $2$ ramifies, matching $\chi_D(2) = 0$. For $p = 2$ and $D \equiv 1 \pmod 4$, apply it to $x^2 - x + \tfrac{1-D}{4}$, the minimal polynomial of $\tfrac{1 + \sqrt D}{2}$: modulo $2$ this is $x(x-1)$ if $D \equiv 1 \pmod 8$ and the irreducible $x^2 + x + 1$ if $D \equiv 5 \pmod 8$, matching $\chi_D(2) = 1$ or $-1$.

The Euler factor of $\zeta_K$ at $p$ is therefore $(1 - p^{-s})^{-2}$, $(1 - p^{-2s})^{-1}$ or $(1 - p^{-s})^{-1}$ in the three cases, and each equals $(1 - p^{-s})^{-1}(1 - \chi_D(p)p^{-s})^{-1}$. Multiplying over $p$ gives the identity, and multiplying the Dirichlet series $\sum m^{-s}$ and $\sum\chi_D(m)m^{-s}$ gives the coefficient formula.

blocks.title: Continuation, functional equation and zeros
blocks.body:
Hecke proved in 1917 that $\zeta_K(s)$ extends to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb C$ whose only pole is a simple pole at $s = 1$, and that it satisfies a functional equation. Let $r_1$ be the number of real embeddings of $K$, $r_2$ the number of pairs of complex ones, $\Gamma_{\mathbb R}(s) = \pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)$ and $\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(s) = 2(2\pi)^{-s}\Gamma(s)$. Then
$$\Lambda_K(s) = |d_K|^{s/2}\,\Gamma_{\mathbb R}(s)^{r_1}\,\Gamma_{\mathbb C}(s)^{r_2}\,\zeta_K(s) \quad\text{satisfies}\quad \Lambda_K(s) = \Lambda_K(1 - s).$$
(Proof omitted; Tate's thesis of 1950 gives the modern proof. For quadratic fields it follows from the factorization and the functional equations of $\zeta$ and $L(s, \chi_D)$, see [[functional-equation]].)

The gamma factors force trivial zeros. For an imaginary quadratic field ($r_1 = 0$, $r_2 = 1$), $\zeta_K$ vanishes at every negative integer and $\zeta_K(0) = -h/w$. For a real quadratic field ($r_1 = 2$), it has double zeros at $-2, -4, -6, \dots$, a simple zero at $0$, and nonzero values at $-1, -3, \dots$. In general $\zeta_K$ has a zero of order $r_1 + r_2 - 1$ at $s = 0$, with leading coefficient $-h_KR_K/w_K$.

All other zeros lie in the critical strip $0 < \mathrm{Re}\,s < 1$, and the generalized Riemann hypothesis for $\zeta_K$ predicts they lie on $\mathrm{Re}\,s = \tfrac12$ (see [[grh]]). For a quadratic field, the nontrivial zeros of $\zeta_K$ are those of $\zeta$ together with those of $L(s, \chi_D)$; a hypothetical [[siegel-zeros|Siegel zero]] of $L(s,\chi_D)$ would be a real zero of $\zeta_K$ very close to $1$.

blocks.title: Analytic class number formula
blocks.body:
$$\mathop{\mathrm{Res}}_{s=1}\zeta_K(s) = \frac{2^{r_1}(2\pi)^{r_2}\,h_K\,R_K}{w_K\sqrt{|d_K|}},$$
where $h_K$ is the class number, $R_K$ the regulator, $w_K$ the number of roots of unity in $K$, and $d_K$ the discriminant. For a quadratic field the residue is $L(1, \chi_D)$, because $\zeta$ has residue $1$, so
$$L(1,\chi_D) = \frac{2\pi h}{w\sqrt{|D|}}\ (D < 0), \qquad L(1, \chi_D) = \frac{2h\log\varepsilon}{\sqrt D}\ (D > 0),$$
with $\varepsilon > 1$ the fundamental unit. (Proof omitted; see Marcus or Neukirch. The idea: the residue equals the density of ideals, $\#\{\mathfrak a : N\mathfrak a \le x\} \sim \mathrm{Res}\cdot x$, and counting ideals class by class reduces to counting lattice points in a region whose volume involves $R_K$ and $\sqrt{|d_K|}$. See also [[class-number-formula]].)

blocks.title: Lattice points on circles and in discs
blocks.body:
(a) How many integer points lie on the circle $x^2 + y^2 = 225$? On $x^2 + y^2 = 5^{10}$?

(b) Explain why the number of integer points $(x, y) \ne (0, 0)$ with $x^2 + y^2 \le X$ is asymptotic to $4L(1, \chi_{-4})X$, and evaluate the constant.
blocks.solution:
(a) Use $r_2(m) = 4\sum_{d \mid m}\chi_{-4}(d)$. The divisors of $225 = 3^2 5^2$ are $1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 25, 45, 75, 225$, with $\chi_{-4}$-values $1, -1, 1, 1, -1, 1, 1, -1, 1$, summing to $3$. So there are $12$ points: $(\pm 15, 0)$, $(0, \pm 15)$, $(\pm 9, \pm 12)$, $(\pm 12, \pm 9)$. For $5^{10}$ all $11$ divisors $5^j$ are $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, so there are $44$ points.

(b) The count is $\sum_{m \le X} r_2(m) = 4\sum_{m \le X}a_K(m)$, and
$$\sum_{m \le X}a_K(m) = \sum_{m \le X}\sum_{d \mid m}\chi_{-4}(d) = \sum_{d \le X}\chi_{-4}(d)\Bigl\lfloor\frac Xd\Bigr\rfloor = X\sum_{d \le X}\frac{\chi_{-4}(d)}{d} + O(\sqrt X).$$
(The error estimate splits the sum at $d = \sqrt X$ and uses that partial sums of $\chi_{-4}$ are bounded.) So the count is $\sim 4L(1, \chi_{-4})X$ with $L(1, \chi_{-4}) = 1 - \tfrac13 + \tfrac15 - \dots = \tfrac\pi4$. The constant $4 \cdot \tfrac\pi4 = \pi$ is the area of the unit disc, as geometry demands; read backwards, the class number formula for $\mathbb Q(i)$ ($h = 1$, $w = 4$, $|D| = 4$) predicts $L(1, \chi_{-4}) = \tfrac{2\pi}{4 \cdot 2} = \tfrac\pi4$, which is Leibniz's series.

blocks.title: Seeing a class number of 2
blocks.body: For $K = \mathbb Q(\sqrt{-5})$ ($D = -20$), compute $a_K(6)$ directly and from the formula, and use the density of ideals to estimate $h_K$ numerically.
blocks.solution:
Directly: the ideals of norm $6$ are products of a prime of norm $2$ and a prime of norm $3$. There is one prime of norm $2$, $P_2 = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$, and two of norm $3$, $P_3 = (3, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$ and $P_3' = (3, 1 - \sqrt{-5})$. So $a_K(6) = 2$: the ideals $P_2P_3 = (1 + \sqrt{-5})$ and $P_2P_3' = (1 - \sqrt{-5})$. From the formula, $\chi_{-20}(1) = 1$, $\chi_{-20}(2) = 0$, $\chi_{-20}(3) = \left(\frac{-20}{3}\right) = 1$, $\chi_{-20}(6) = 0$, total $2$.

Density: as in the previous example, $\#\{\mathfrak a : N\mathfrak a \le X\} = \sum_{d \le X}\chi_{-20}(d)\lfloor X/d\rfloor \approx L(1,\chi_{-20})X$. Numerically, for $X = 10^5$ the ratio is about $1.405$, while $\tfrac{\pi}{\sqrt 5} \approx 1.4050$. The class number formula with $w = 2$, $|D| = 20$ reads $L(1, \chi_{-20}) = \tfrac{2\pi h}{2\sqrt{20}} = \tfrac{\pi h}{2\sqrt 5}$, so the measured density gives $h \approx 2$, the class number found in [[class-group]].

blocks.title: Special values
blocks.body: Compute $\zeta_{\mathbb Q(i)}(0)$ and $\zeta_{\mathbb Q(\sqrt 5)}(-1)$, and compare $\zeta_{\mathbb Q(i)}(0)$ with $-h/w$.
blocks.solution:
We use $\zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$, $\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac1{12}$, and the formula $L(1 - k, \chi) = -B_{k,\chi}/k$ with generalized Bernoulli numbers $B_{k,\chi} = q^{k-1}\sum_{a=1}^{q}\chi(a)B_k(a/q)$ for a character modulo $q$, where $B_1(x) = x - \tfrac12$ and $B_2(x) = x^2 - x + \tfrac16$.

For $\chi_{-4}$: $B_{1,\chi} = \chi(1)B_1(\tfrac14) + \chi(3)B_1(\tfrac34) = -\tfrac14 - \tfrac14 = -\tfrac12$, so $L(0, \chi_{-4}) = \tfrac12$ and $\zeta_{\mathbb Q(i)}(0) = -\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = -\tfrac14$. This equals $-h/w = -\tfrac14$, as it should.

For $\chi_5$ (values $1, -1, -1, 1$ at $1, 2, 3, 4$): the constant terms of $B_2$ cancel since $\sum\chi(a) = 0$, and $\sum\chi(a)a = 1 - 2 - 3 + 4 = 0$, so $B_{2,\chi} = 5\cdot\tfrac1{25}\sum\chi(a)a^2 = \tfrac15(1 - 4 - 9 + 16) = \tfrac45$. Hence $L(-1, \chi_5) = -\tfrac25$ and
$$\zeta_{\mathbb Q(\sqrt 5)}(-1) = \Bigl(-\frac1{12}\Bigr)\Bigl(-\frac25\Bigr) = \frac1{30}.$$
That this value is rational is an instance of the Siegel–Klingen theorem for totally real fields.

blocks.body:
- The character is $\chi_D$ for the discriminant $D$, not $\left(\frac d\cdot\right)$ for the squarefree $d$: for $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-5})$ one needs the character modulo $20$, which is $0$ at $2$ because $2$ ramifies.
- $\zeta_K$ counts ideals, not elements. In $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-5})$ the number of ideals of norm $m$ is not the number of solutions of $x^2 + 5y^2 = m$ divided by $2$; non-principal ideals are counted too (for $m = 3$ there are two ideals and no elements).
- Factoring $\zeta_K$ into Dirichlet $L$-functions works for abelian fields such as quadratic and cyclotomic ones, not in general. For $K = \mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)$, $\zeta_K(s)/\zeta(s)$ is an $L$-function attached to a cubic Hecke character of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$, not a product of Dirichlet $L$-functions.
- The functional equation relates $s$ and $1 - s$ for the completed function $\Lambda_K$; $\zeta_K$ itself is not symmetric.

- Replacing the norm by a character on ideals gives [[hecke-l]] functions; $\zeta_K$ is the case of the trivial character, and $\zeta_K(s)L(s, \psi)$ products describe extensions of $K$. The example $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)$ above ties back to [[cubic-characters]]: a prime $p \equiv 1 \pmod 3$ splits completely in $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)$ exactly when $2$ is a cube modulo $p$.
- The residue at $s = 1$ is the analytic class number formula ([[class-number-formula]]), the main tool for estimating class numbers ([[class-group]]) and the reason [[siegel-zeros]] matter.
- For cyclotomic fields, $\zeta_{\mathbb Q(\zeta_n)}$ is the product of the $L$-functions of the primitive characters behind the characters modulo $n$ (see [[cyclotomic]], [[l-functions]]); its pole at $s = 1$ is one way to prove $L(1, \chi) \ne 0$.
- The generalized Riemann hypothesis for $\zeta_K$ is part of [[grh]].

1. Write down the Euler factors of $\zeta_{\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})}$ at $p = 2, 3, 7$ and check that each equals $(1 - p^{-s})^{-1}(1 - \chi_{-3}(p)p^{-s})^{-1}$.
2. Deduce from $\zeta_{\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})} = \zeta(s)L(s,\chi_{-3})$ that the number of integer pairs with $a^2 - ab + b^2 = m$ is $6\sum_{d \mid m}\chi_{-3}(d)$.
3. Show that the number of ideals of norm $p^k$ in a quadratic field is $k + 1$, $1$ or $0$, or $1$, according as $p$ splits, is inert ($k$ even or odd), or ramifies.
4. Compute $L(1, \chi_{-7})$ numerically and use the class number formula to confirm $h(-7) = 1$.
